title: Walk in Truth and Love; Beware the Deceiver
summary: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, rejoicing that some of them walk in the truth and reminding them of the commandment they have had from the beginning, that we love one another. He warns that many deceivers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh have gone out into the world, and he tells the church not to welcome such teachers into their home. He closes with the hope of seeing them face to face.
story: Second John applies the message of First John to a single congregation. The deceivers who went out from John's community (1 John 2:19) are now traveling, and they depend on the hospitality of churches to spread their message. This short letter arms one house church to receive them wisely. It follows the pattern of an ordinary ancient letter: sender, recipient, greeting, body, and closing. In the Bible's story, it shows the church at the end of the apostolic age learning to guard the truth about Christ while keeping love as its law.
historical:
The letter comes from the same setting as First John: churches in the Roman province of Asia, traditionally linked with the apostle John in Ephesus, late in the first century. The writer calls himself simply the elder, a title that could describe an older man, a church leader, or a senior figure recognized across many congregations. Tradition identified him as the apostle John; some scholars think he was a different leader named John, sometimes connected with the John the elder mentioned by Papias in the early second century.

The central problem is described in verse 7: many deceivers who refuse to confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh. This is the same teaching First John opposes, very likely an early form of docetism, which held that the divine Christ only seemed to be human. Verse 9 describes these teachers as ones who run ahead, which suggests that they presented their teaching as a more advanced stage of faith, beyond what the church had first received.
cultural:
Early churches met in homes, and a home was both a place of worship and a base for mission. Traveling teachers relied on believers to give them lodging, meals, and supplies for the next leg of their trip. To welcome someone into one's house church was to give them a platform in that congregation and a kind of endorsement. That is why the elder's instruction is so pointed: do not receive such a person into your home or even greet him (verse 10). The greeting he has in mind is likely the formal welcome and blessing given to a guest teacher, which signaled fellowship and support.

Letters were written on sheets of papyrus with reed pens and ink, and a short letter like this one would fit on a single sheet. The elder's wish to speak face to face (verse 12) reflects a common feeling in ancient letters that writing was a second-best substitute for presence. The chosen lady may be a real woman who led or hosted a church, or a figure for the church itself, with her children as its members and her elect sister (verse 13) as the church where the elder lived. Both readings have ancient and modern defenders.
literary: The letter has the shape of a Greco-Roman personal letter, but its vocabulary is the vocabulary of First John: truth, love, commandment, from the beginning, walk, remain, antichrist, the Father and the Son. Truth appears five times in the first four verses, and it frames the whole greeting. Verses 4-6 tie love and obedience together in a loop: love is walking in his commands, and the command is to walk in love. Verses 7-11 turn to warning, marked by the repetition of teaching (didache). The letter ends, like Third John, with the elder's wish for a visit rather than more writing, and with greetings from the sister church.

outline.t: Greeting: truth, love, grace, mercy, and peace
Walking in truth and in the old commandment of love
Deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh
Hope of a visit and final greetings

doctrines.note: The confession that Jesus Christ came in the flesh is the dividing line between truth and deception. Whoever remains in the teaching of Christ has both the Father and the Son (verse 9).

The church is pictured as a family, a lady and her children, with sister churches linked by greetings. Its life is ordered by truth and love, and it must guard its fellowship from teaching that denies Christ.
Love and obedience are not rivals. This is love, that we walk according to his commandments, and the commandment is that we walk in love (verse 6). The command is old, heard from the beginning.

words.note: Aletheia, truth, used five times in this short letter. For the elder, truth is not only accurate statement but reality as God has revealed it in Christ. It abides in believers, they walk in it, and it is the ground of their love for one another.

Didache, teaching. The teaching of Christ in verse 9 may mean the teaching about Christ or the teaching Christ himself gave; both fit. Whoever does not remain in it but runs ahead does not have God. The same word later named an early Christian manual, the Didache.

Planos, deceiver, one who leads others astray. The related verb describes wandering off course. The elder uses it for teachers whose denial of the incarnation leads people away from the truth, and he joins it with the word antichrist.

christ: The letter shows Christ as the Son of the Father, the source, together with the Father, of grace, mercy, and peace (verse 3). Most of all it insists that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. The incarnation is not negotiable: those who deny it are deceivers, and those who go beyond the teaching of Christ lose God himself. To remain in that teaching is to have both the Father and the Son. The letter's two commands, to love and to hold the truth, meet in Christ, who is himself truth and who commanded his disciples to love one another.

hard.q: Isn't it unloving to refuse even to greet someone who holds a different view?
hard.a:
The instruction in verses 10-11 has troubled many readers, and it has sometimes been used to justify cutting off anyone who disagrees. In context its scope is narrow. It concerns traveling teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, a denial the elder regards as abandoning God himself, and who come seeking hospitality as a base for spreading that teaching. To welcome them into the house church and give them the customary blessing would be to share in their work, as verse 11 says.

Interpreters differ on how far the principle extends. Some apply it to any teacher who denies core Christian truth, such as the deity or humanity of Christ. Others stress that it concerns public sponsorship by a church, not ordinary courtesy to individuals, and they note that the same letter commands love. Few think it forbids kindness to unbelievers, conversation with doubters, or hospitality to those who disagree on second-order matters. The elder's concern is that love must not become a door through which a false Christ enters the church.

questions: The elder says love is walking in God's commands. How does that definition challenge the way love is usually talked about?
What would it look like for a church today to be both open-handed in hospitality and careful about whose message it endorses?
The deceivers are described as running ahead of the teaching of Christ. Where do you see the pull toward a more advanced faith that leaves Christ behind?
